title: SRE SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, and Runbooks — Standards & Playbook
author: Ari Chen
content:
Overview:

This document defines Redwood Inference's SRE standards and playbook for Service Level Objectives (SLOs) and Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, Reliability Initiatives, Incident Review standards, Operational Tooling, and Runbook templates. It is intended for on-call SREs, service owners, and platform engineers. Follow these standards to ensure consistent measurement, escalation, and remediation across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.

1) Principles and scope
- Principles:
  - Users-first: SLOs should reflect customer experience and product-level expectations (latency, correctness where applicable, and availability).
  - Measurable & actionable: Metrics used for SLOs must be instrumented, documented, and wired into dashboards and alerts.
  - Ownership: Each SLO has a named owner responsible for maintaining the SLO, the associated alerting, and the error budget policy.
  - Incremental improvement: Use error budget policy to guide rollouts, feature flags, and reliability work.
- Scope: Applies to all production services in the Redwood Inference stack (runtime, router, control plane, dedicated pools, private deployment components).

2) SLO taxonomy and examples
- Types of SLOs we maintain:
  - Availability SLOs (percentage of successful user-facing requests).
  - Latency SLOs (p50/p90/p95/p99 for request types; generation tokens per second where appropriate).
  - Correctness/Quality SLOs (for rerankers, classifier thresholds, or regression-detected model quality drops).
  - Throughput SLOs (sustained requests/sec or tokens/sec per capacity unit).

- Representative SLO table (use this as a template):

|Metric|Target|Window|Owner|SLI definition|Alert threshold|
|-----|------|:----:|-----|--------------|---------------|
|API latency (text-generation p95)|<= 250 ms|30d|serving-runtime|p95 of end-to-end request latency excluding long-polling|p95 > 300ms for 15m|
|Availability (hosted API, error rate)|>= 99.95%|30d|eng-sre|fraction of requests with 5xx or defined error codes|error_rate > 0.15% sustained 15m|
|Embeddings throughput per GPU|>= 500 req/s|7d|eng-infra|successful embeddings/sec normalized by GPU pool size|throughput < 400 req/s for 1h|

Notes:
- SLI definitions must reference the exact metric name and tags used in monitoring (e.g., telemetry.request.latency_ms{route=/v1/generate,model=redwood-v2}).
- Record the SLI query and the Prometheus/Grafana dashboard ID in the SLO page for the service.

3) Error budget policy and burn actions
- Error budget calculation: Error budget = (1 - SLO_target) * SLO_window_total_requests (or percentage over the window).
- Burn rate windows: Monitor both short-term (1h, 6h) and long-term (7d, 30d) burn rates to detect fast and slow burns.
- Standard actions keyed to burn rate:
  1. Normal (burn_rate <= 1x): Continue normal operations; track in weekly reliability board.
  2. Elevated (1x < burn_rate <= 3x): Service owner must convene a short reliability review; pause unsafe rollouts; prioritize quick mitigations.
  3. Critical (burn_rate > 3x or error budget exhausted): Trigger incident process, halt feature rollouts and A/B tests, schedule post-incident review within 3 business days.
- Rollout control: CI/CD pipelines must respect an "error_budget_guard" check that can be toggled by SRE to block dangerous rollouts when error budget is critical.

4) Capacity planning and sizing guidance
- Key inputs for capacity plans:
  - Traffic forecasts by customer segment, model, and route (monthly and weekly granularity).
  - Per-request resource cost (tokens, compute time, GPU memory).
  - Desired headroom target (default N+30% for bursty models; configurable per service).
  - Recovery time objectives for scaling events (target cold-start < 60s).
- Process (quarterly / event-driven):
  1. Collect telemetry baseline for the lookback period (90 days).
  2. Forecast demand for next quarter using growth signals from product and sales.
  3. Convert demand to capacity units (GPU-hours, worker count).
  4. Run what-if simulations for model rollouts, quantization changes, and region failover.
  5. Publish capacity plan and required procurement/booking by the start of the quarter.
- Autoscaling & throttling rules:
  - Define per-pool autoscale policies with min/max instances, cooldown windows, and scaling step sizes.
  - Use workload-aware batching to optimize throughput for high-volume low-latency workloads.

5) Reliability initiatives and roadmap alignment
- Types of reliability work:
  - Incident remediation and blameless postmortems (P1/P2 correctness).
  - Proactive investments: improved SLIs, traffic shaping, circuit breakers, smart routing policies.
  - Performance engineering: kernel tuning, batching improvements, quantization profiles.
- Prioritization: Use an "impact x effort" matrix and tie each initiative to expected error budget-week savings or latency improvement. Track initiatives on the reliability board with owners and target milestones.

6) Incident review and postmortem standards
- When to run a postmortem: All incidents that cross P0/P1 thresholds or exhaust an error budget require a formal postmortem published in Confluence within 3 business days.
- Postmortem structure (required):
  - Title, incident window, severity, services affected, detection and mitigation timeline.
  - Root cause analysis (5 whys / causal graph).
  - Impact quantification (user-facing metrics, customer tickets, financial impact if known).
  - Action items with owners and due dates (minimum: one remediation and one systemic prevention).
  - Error budget impact and whether rollback of recent changes would have prevented the issue.
- Review cycle: Postmortems are reviewed in the monthly reliability review and associated action items are tracked until completion.

7) Runbook templates and on-call playbooks
- Runbook template (fill for each critical service):
  - Service name: 
  - Pager channel: #pager-service-name
  - On-call owner: (team/person)
  - SLOs and SLIs (link)
  - Known failure modes (brief list)
  - Immediate triage steps (numbered):
    1. Check dashboards: SLI overview, recent deploys, error logs.
    2. If error rate spike: run 'ci/bin/roll-back-last-deploy --service <svc>'.
    3. If latency spike on specific route: isolate by toggling routing policy to canary fallback model: 'adminctl route set-fallback <route> <model-variant>'.
    4. If capacity pressure: scale GPU pool via terraform or autoscaler API: 'infra autoscale --pool <name> --add 2'.
    5. If degraded third-party dependency: enable circuit breaker and retry with exponential backoff.
  - Escalation matrix: primary on-call -> service owner -> eng-sre lead -> head of platform.
  - Post-incident checklist: create postmortem, notify customers (if affected), schedule reliability review.

- Example CLI snippets (for runbook use):
  - Check p95 latency in Prometheus: curl -s "https://prometheus/api/v1/query?query=histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_latency_seconds_bucket{service=\"svc\"}[5m])) by (le))"
  - Roll back last deploy: ci/bin/rollback --service svc --to-tag <previous-tag>

8) Operational tooling and observability requirements
- Minimum tooling for every service:
  - Metrics: Prometheus metrics for request counts, error counts, latency buckets, GPU utilization, queue lengths.
  - Tracing: Distributed traces for request end-to-end path (sampling guidelines documented per service).
  - Logging: Structured JSON logs with request_id, trace_id, model, customer_tier. Logs index in centralized ELK/Opensearch with 90-day retention by default.
  - Dashboards: One SLO dashboard and one Triage dashboard per service (p95/p99, error-rate trend, deploy timeline, capacity utilization).
  - Alerting: PagerDuty integration for critical alerts; Slack for lower-severity notifications. Alerts must include runbook link and relevant diagnostic queries.
  - Chaos and soak testing: Periodic game days and chaos experiments for critical failure modes; track results in post-game reports.

9) Ownership and governance
- SLO owner: Service owner (product or platform) is accountable for target selection and SLO maintenance. Eng-SRE provides audit and guidance.
- Review cadence: Quarterly SLO review meetings where owners justify targets, SLIs, and any changes. Changes to SLO targets must be approved by eng-sre and documented with rationale.
- Audit: Eng-SRE runs an annual SLO audit and publishes findings (gaps, missing dashboards, or unmaintained runbooks).

10) Templates and checklist appendix
- Runbook checklist (must be present for all services classified as Tier 1 or Tier 2):
  - SLO links present
  - On-call escalation defined
  - Runbook steps validated in last 90 days
  - Dashboard view link present
  - CI rollback playbook validated

- SLO change request checklist:
  1. Document current SLO and SLIs.
  2. Provide reason for change (customer feedback, cost optimization, new feature).
  3. Show impact analysis (error budget, customer experience).
  4. Reviewer approvals from eng-sre and service owner.
